---
title: "Sigma-algebras"
---

If a model assigns a probability to the event that a token has lemma *ne*, which other events must it measure? It must include the complement, and it must keep unions of measurable events available. We call this requirement the **closure problem**.

Basically, we solve the closure problem by collecting events in a way that never strands us without a required complement or union. More specifically, a [**sigma-algebra**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces), also called an event space, is a collection $\mathcal F$ that contains the sample space and is closed under complements and countable unions.

```{r}
#| label: load-event-space-data
library(ggplot2)

wh <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
wh$outcome_id <- paste(wh$split, wh$sentence_id, wh$token_id, sep = ":")
omega <- wh$outcome_id
N <- omega[wh$lemma == "ne"]
O <- omega[wh$dependency_relation == "obj"]

stopifnot(nrow(wh) == 167L, !anyDuplicated(omega))
```

## A one-generator event space

The sigma-algebra generated by $N$ is

$$
\mathcal F_N
\equiv
\sigma(N)
=
\{\varnothing,N,N^c,\Omega\}.
$$

It contains exactly the unions of the two atoms $N$ and $N^c$. This event space can represent whether the lemma is *ne*, but it cannot distinguish *hangi* from *kim* inside $N^c$.

## Closure requirements

A collection $\mathcal F$ is a sigma-algebra only if:

1. $\Omega\in\mathcal F$;
2. if $B\in\mathcal F$, then $B^c\in\mathcal F$;
3. if $B_1,B_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F$, then $\bigcup_iB_i\in\mathcal F$.

The impossible event follows from the first two requirements:

$$
\Omega^c=\varnothing\in\mathcal F.
$$

Intersections follow from complements and unions by De Morgan's law:

$$
B\cap C=(B^c\cup C^c)^c.
$$

Thus closure under complements and countable unions also gives closure under intersections.

## Two generators and their atoms

The events $N$ and $O$ split the observed token space into the four nonempty atoms

$$
N\cap O,
\quad
N\cap O^c,
\quad
N^c\cap O,
\quad
N^c\cap O^c.
$$

Every event in $\sigma(N,O)$ is a union of these atoms.

```{r}
#| label: construct-event-space-atoms
wh$atom <- interaction(
  ifelse(wh$ne_lemma == 1, "ne", "other"),
  ifelse(wh$object == 1, "obj", "nsubj"),
  sep = " & ", drop = TRUE
)
atom_counts <- as.data.frame(table(wh$atom), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(atom_counts) <- c("atom", "tokens")

atom_number <- nrow(atom_counts)
event_number <- 2^atom_number

stopifnot(
  all(atom_counts$tokens > 0),
  sum(atom_counts$tokens) == nrow(wh),
  event_number == length(unlist(
    lapply(0:atom_number, function(k) combn(atom_number, k, simplify = FALSE)),
    recursive = FALSE
  ))
)

c(atoms = atom_number, measurable_events = event_number)
```

The observed generators produce `r atom_number` nonempty atoms and thus `r event_number` measurable unions. These values are derived from the attested cross-classification rather than stipulated for instruction.

```{r}
#| label: plot-event-space-atoms
#| fig-cap: "Empirical sizes of the atoms that generate the event space."
ggplot(atom_counts, aes(reorder(atom, tokens), tokens)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey65") +
  geom_point(color = "#2C7FB8", size = 2) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Tokens") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## A collection that fails closure

Consider

$$
\mathcal G\equiv\{\Omega,N\}.
$$

It contains $\Omega$, but it omits $N^c$ and $\varnothing$. Thus it is not a sigma-algebra. Adding those two required events yields $\mathcal F_N$.

A subset of $\Omega$ need not belong to a particular sigma-algebra. For instance, the singleton containing one observed *ne* token is a subset of $\Omega$ but is not a member of $\mathcal F_N$. The model represents the token as an outcome while declining to assign a separate probability to that singleton. For finite course examples we will often use the power set $2^\Omega$, but that is a modeling choice rather than part of the definition of a sample space.

$\Omega$ lists outcomes, while $\mathcal F$ lists outcome groupings that can receive probabilities. The [next page](generating-event-spaces.qmd) constructs the smallest event space forced by a richer set of linguistic distinctions.

## Check your understanding

1. Starting from $\{\Omega,N\}$, name the two events closure requires.
2. Use `atom_counts` to identify the largest atom. Which lemma and relation properties define it?
3. Why does a singleton token subset fail to belong to $\mathcal F_N$ even though it belongs to $2^\Omega$?
4. Use De Morgan's law to express $N\cap O$ using only complements and a union.

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Starting from $\{\Omega,N\}$, closure adds $N^c$ and $\varnothing$, yielding $\{\varnothing,N,N^c,\Omega\}$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The largest atom is $N\cap O$, the 112 tokens whose lemma is *ne* and whose dependency relation is `obj`. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. A singleton token is in $2^\Omega$ but not in $\mathcal F_N$ because $\mathcal F_N$ distinguishes only the complete *ne* and non-*ne* atoms, not individual tokens. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. De Morgan's law gives $N\cap O=(N^c\cup O^c)^c$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
